text:
CHAIN:
L1: Add `gate = nn.Linear(384,128)` and set latent = `latent_norm(compress(x) * silu(gate(x)))`. This makes the latent channel profile depend on the token rather than being a fixed linear image of it | quantity: across-token coefficient of variation of `silu(gate(x))` per channel, plus the share of latent energy in each token's top 16 of 128 channels | baseline: unmeasured (the current latent has no gate; the top-16 share of the ungated `latent_norm(compress(x))` is the comparison) | expect: CV clearly above 0.1 in most layers; top-16 share up vs the ungated latent at the matched step | breaks if: the gate CV stays below about 0.1, or one channel profile is shared across tokens. Per-token RMSNorm cancels any uniform gate, so such a gate is a no-op.

L2: A selective latent gives K/V more usable per-channel information, so attention retrieves context better | quantity: recall-token loss (bigram already seen in the window); late-minus-early position gap | baseline: 4.475 at step 100; gap +0.459 | expect: recall loss lower by 0.02 to 0.10 at step 100; gap no wider | breaks if: recall-token loss at step 100 is within ±0.02 of 4.475 over 3 seeds.

L3: The extra nonlinearity does not slow early learning. At std 0.02 init, the latent starts roughly bilinear, i.e. not the old linear code | quantity: loss at steps 26 and 51 | baseline: 7.0622, 6.5902 | expect: within ±0.03 or lower | breaks if: step-26 loss is more than 0.03 above the baseline on all seeds.

L4: Better context coding shows up most on rare targets | quantity: loss on rank 10000–50304 tokens | baseline: 11.613 at step 100 | expect: 0 to −0.03, smaller in relative terms than the recall-token gain | breaks if: rare-token loss is flat while recall-token loss falls. That would mean the effect is real but mis-targeted.

L5: The sum of L2 and L4 gives a lower exam loss after 50M tokens | quantity: exam val loss from model.pt | baseline: pooled baseline mean (not given here) | expect: lower by 0.005 to 0.02 nats | breaks if: one-sided Welch p ≥ 0.01 over 3 or more seeds, or the gain is ≤ 0.005.

WEAKEST: L2. Nothing measured shows that the 128-dim latent limits this model at 21M params and 50M tokens. A half-rank latent cost only about 0.3% loss at 30M params (https://arxiv.org/html/2506.09342v2).

QUESTIONS:

Q1: Is the 128-dim latent a real bottleneck here, or would the same 49k params per layer do more as a wider linear latent? | decides: gated 128-dim latent vs ungated latent widened to about 170 (42 × (384+768) = 48.4k params per layer, equal budget)
A1: Unknown. The only small-scale evidence says a half-rank latent costs about 0.3% loss vs MHA (https://arxiv.org/html/2506.09342v2). Here the latent is a third of d, so the bottleneck is plausible but unproven. The builder should run the equal-param wider latent as the control arm. Without it, a win cannot be credited to nonlinearity.

Q2: silu gate at default std-0.02 init, or 2·sigmoid gate with zero-initialised `W_g` (identical to the current model at step 0)? | decides: `silu(W_g x)` with `_init` std 0.02 vs `2*sigmoid(W_g x)` with `W_g` zeroed
A2: The input x is the RMS-normed read with RMS about 1. `W_g x` therefore has std about 0.02·√384 ≈ 0.39, where silu(z) ≈ z/2 + z²/4. At init the latent is roughly the product of two independent random projections. The linear code the current model starts from is gone, and the latent's sign depends on `W_g x`. RMSNorm cancels the overall 0.5 scale but not this. A zero-init 2·sigmoid gate starts as the current model exactly, because a uniform gate is erased by the latent norm, and then learns relative selection. The spec says silu ("do not water it down"), so build silu. L3 (step-26 loss) is the check that tells whether the init cost matters.

Q3: Which variant: gate on the input before the norm (the idea), or gated expansion `expand(c)*silu(gate(c))` (the alternative)? | decides: 384→128 gate before `latent_norm` vs 128→768 gate after it
A3: Choose the input gate. Its output passes through `latent_norm`, so V's scale stays at about 0.02·√128 ≈ 0.23 as now. The expansion gate multiplies V, which is not normed, by silu of a std-0.23 signal (≈ 0.12). That shrinks V and the attention output about 8x at init, on top of the already small `wo` init. The expansion gate also costs twice the params (98k per layer).

Q4: Can a 45-step smoke run resolve a 0.01-nat difference? | decides: kill on mean loss over steps 40–45 vs kill on matched-step loss at step 100–150 over 2–3 seeds
A4: Probably not. At step 45 (about 1.5M tokens) the loss is around 6.6 and falling fast. Layer-0 attention entropy is 0.957 (near flat) even at step 100, so attention carries little of the loss that early. Seed-to-seed spread at step 45 is unmeasured. The kill should use the step-100 recall-token loss and overall loss across seeds. The step-45 run stays as a crash and VRAM check.

Q5: Should the target metric be rare-token loss or recall-token loss? | decides: which diagnostic the smoke run logs and kills on
A5: Use recall tokens. The K/V being changed belong to context tokens, and they affect a target only through attention. Rare-target loss (11.613, 12% of tokens) is dominated by unigram and output-embedding learning at this stage. Recall tokens (13% of targets, 4.475) are the attention-dependent class. Keep rare-token loss as a secondary readout.

Q6: All 12 layers, or the first few? | decides: gate in every block vs gate only in block 0 (or blocks 0–1)
A6: Unknown which wins. The layer-0 input is the RMS-normed token embedding, because the four streams are identical copies and the read weights sum to 1. So the layer-0 gate is a nonlinear per-token K/V code, freed from the tied input/output embedding geometry. Layer-0 attention gradient is also an outlier (0.24–0.29 vs about 0.02 in its neighbours, z 7.03 on 3 seeds). Build all layers as specified, but log per-layer gate CV to see where the gate is used.

Q7: Should the gate act on the whole shared latent (K and V) or only the V half? | decides: one shared gated latent vs gating only the V slice of `expand` output
A7: The idea keeps one latent shared by K and V, so gating it gates both. K then passes through `k_norm`, which partly absorbs the gate. In Qwen's gated-attention study, gating after the value projection helped less than gating the SDPA output. I recall this from https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06708 and have not re-checked it. Build the shared gate per spec.

Q8: Which optimizer group does `W_g` land in, and does that matter? | decides: Muon (automatic) vs explicit AdamW
A8: It is 2-D and its name contains neither "tok" nor "head", so `build_optimizers` puts it in Muon automatically with shape scale max(1, 128/384)^0.5 = 1. The latent RMSNorm makes the forward pass invariant to the gate's overall scale. Its backward pass amplifies gradients by 1/rms(input), but Muon's orthogonalised update hides gradient scale anyway. No change is needed.

KNOWN:
- Current attention per layer: `wq` 384×576 (221,184), `compress` 384×128 (49,152), `latent_norm` 128, `expand` 128×768 (98,304), `rotary` 384×32 (12,288), q/k norms 128, `wo` 384×384 (147,456); total 528,640 [script]
- Per block 1,770,160 non-embedding params; 12 blocks plus final norm ≈ 21.242M, which matches the stated 21.24M baseline. The cap is about 23.37M, leaving about 2.12M headroom [script]
- An MHA baseline with d_ff=1024 also gives 21.24M (1,770,240 per block). Parameter count alone cannot tell whether the measurements are of the MHA baseline or of this MLA script [belief]
- The gate adds 49,152 params per layer, 589,824 total, giving about 21.83M, inside the cap [script]
- Plug-in point: `Attention.__init__` adds `self.gate = nn.Linear(cfg.d_model, 128, bias=False)`; `forward` changes `kv = self.expand(self.latent_norm(self.compress(x) * F.silu(self.gate(x))))`. Nothing else changes: `_init` gives std 0.02, and Muon picks it up [script]
- `latent_norm` is per-token RMSNorm over the 128 channels. Any gate that scales all channels equally for a token has no effect; only relative across-channel gating survives [belief]
- At init, `gate(x)` has std about 0.39, so silu works in its near-quadratic region, and the latent at init is about half the elementwise product of two random projections [belief]
- V is not normed: v RMS ≈ 0.02·√128 ≈ 0.23 at init, and the input-gate design leaves this unchanged [belief]
- Extra FLOPs ≈ 0.59M MACs per token against about 21M in blocks plus 19.3M in the tied head (50304×384), so roughly 1.5% before elementwise ops [belief]
- Extra saved activations ≈ 3 × 128 bf16 per token per layer, about 9 KB per token. At 4096 tokens per micro-batch that is about 38 MB, negligible against the 5.6 GB limit. Baseline peak VRAM is not reported [belief]
- Layer-0 attention gradient is 0.2406 vs 0.0195–0.0339 in other layers; the anomaly replicates on 3 seeds (z 7.03) [measured]
- Recall tokens: 13% of targets, loss 4.475 vs 6.704 for the rest at step 100 [measured]
- Rare tokens (rank 10000–50304): 12% of tokens, loss 11.613 at step 100 [measured]
- First-token attention mass is 0.002–0.006 in all layers, so there is no attention sink to fix [measured]
- MLA without RoPE trailed MHA by 3–5% at 30M params. The decoupled rotary path here bypasses the latent, so the gate does not touch positional information (https://arxiv.org/html/2506.09342v2) [web]
- The decoupled shared rotary sub-vector was the only MLA variant that avoided rank collapse in a spectral analysis (https://arxiv.org/html/2507.09394v1) [web]
- Value-position gating helped less than SDPA-output gating (from memory of https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06708, not re-checked) [belief]

ASSUMES:
- The 128-dim latent limits quality at 21M params, 50M tokens and context 1024. Rank is the constraint, not training time.
- Spending 49k params per layer on nonlinearity beats spending them on more latent width.
- Losing the linear latent at init (silu in its near-quadratic regime) costs less than the expressiveness gained.
- K/V of position t should depend only on the residual at t.
- K and V should share one gated code, and all six heads should see the same gate.
- The effect appears within 45 steps and is concentrated on rare targets.
- The gate is useful in every layer, not mainly at layer 0, where the input is the bare embedding.

NEW IDEAS:

SLOT: drop
IDEA: Previous-token-gated latent
MECHANISM: Drop "K/V at t depend only on x_t". Use latent = norm(W_c x_t ⊙ silu(W_g x_{t−1})), with x_{t−1} a causal shift by one position and zero at t=0. The KV code then directly carries "which token preceded me", which is the key an induction head matches on.
PREDICTION: Recall-token loss falls faster than with the same-token gate, and late-position loss improves relative to early positions.
TEST: 100 steps × 2 seeds. Compare recall-token loss and the late-minus-early gap against baseline (4.475, +0.459) and against the same-token gate.
SOURCE: own (token-shift in the spirit of RWKV)
PART: Sequence mixing: latent KV compression and expansion
KIND: leap
BREAKS: Keys and values at position t are functions of position t's residual only.
KILL: Step-100 recall-token loss not below 4.475 by at least 0.05 averaged over 2 seeds, or step-100 overall loss above baseline.

SLOT: strengthen
IDEA: Per-head gates over the shared latent
MECHANISM: Keep one 128-dim normed latent c. Each head h gets its own gate g_h = 2·sigmoid(W_h c) through a single 128→768 map (98k params per layer, 1.18M total, within headroom), and `expand` acts per head on c ⊙ g_h. This lets the six heads read different subsets of the shared code.
PREDICTION: Lower recall-token loss than the shared gate; head-to-head similarity of K drops.
TEST: Build-only (≤ 23.37M), then 100-step matched run vs the shared-gate build.
SOURCE: https://arxiv.org/html/2601.11471v2 (head diversity via per-head deviation from shared KV)
PART: Sequence mixing: latent KV compression and expansion
KIND: port

SLOT: specialise
IDEA: Layer-0-only gated latent
MECHANISM: Apply the gate only in block 0, where the input is the bare token embedding. There the gate acts as a learned nonlinear per-token K/V code, decoupled from the tied embedding geometry. The other 11 layers stay linear.
PREDICTION: The layer-0 attention gradient (0.24) moves toward its neighbours; loss at step 100 matches or beats the all-layer gate at 1/12 of the param cost.
TEST: 100-step run, 2 seeds. Compare the layer-0 grad norm and overall loss with the all-layer build.
SOURCE: own
PART: Sequence mixing: latent KV compression and expansion
KIND: port

SLOT: port
IDEA: Token-dependent stream read
MECHANISM: Port the same "make a fixed linear map input-conditional" step to the residual-stream read. Read weights become softmax(read_logits + W_r · norm(mean of streams)) per token, with `W_r` 384→4 zero-initialised. This restores the dynamic part of hyper-connections that the recipe replaced with static logits.
PREDICTION: Lower loss at step 100; read weights vary across tokens (entropy spread > 0).
TEST: Build-only, then a 100-step matched run.
SOURCE: https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.19606
PART: Residual streams (static 4-stream Sinkhorn mixing)
KIND: port

SLOT: combine
IDEA: Gated latent + head-wise SDPA output gate
MECHANISM: Keep the gated latent and add a per-head scalar gate y_h ← y_h · sigmoid(w_h·x) (384→6, 2.3k params per layer) before `wo`. This adds a nonlinearity between V and `wo`, which are otherwise one low-rank linear product. The full 384→384 gate would exceed the remaining headroom together with the latent gate.
PREDICTION: The gains add up: overall loss below the latent-gate-only build at step 100.
TEST: 100-step, 2-seed comparison of latent-gate-only vs combined.
SOURCE: https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06708
PART: Sequence mixing: latent KV compression and expansion
KIND: port
